explanations.explanation: That's what verse 1 says: these women oppress the poor and crush the needy. Those are the people getting pressed down. Then they turn to their husbands and say, "Bring us more to drink." I think that tells you a lot about where their attention was.

Priests and prophets sound official, friend, but Amos doesn't name them here. The verse says the ones being oppressed and crushed are the poor and the needy. When a question points at one verse, the verse has the answer. Check it before you trust the fancy-sounding option.

Kings and princes make a grand-sounding list, and I grab the grand-sounding answer too sometimes. But verse 1 doesn't mention them. The women oppress the poor and crush the needy. Amos points to people with little, not people at the top.

explanations.answer: They will be taken away with hooks
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. The Lord GOD swears by His holiness that they will be taken away with hooks, and their posterity with fishhooks (Amos 4:2). Posterity means the ones who come after them. He swears it by His holiness, so this isn't a small warning.

explanations.answer: They will be crowned in Samaria
explanations.explanation: Crowned in Samaria sounds like a party with good lighting. But that's not what the Lord GOD says. He says the days are coming when they will be taken away with hooks. No crowns in that verse.

explanations.answer: They will be given more land
explanations.explanation: More land would be a lovely surprise, like finding an extra bag of chocolate chips in the pantry. But the oath says the opposite. These women will be taken away with hooks, and their posterity with fishhooks. Taken away, not handed more.

True. The LORD says, "You will go out through broken walls, each one straight ahead of her…" (Amos 4:3). So the walls are broken, and each woman goes straight ahead. After that, they are cast out toward Harmon.

It's actually True, friend. The LORD says they will go out through broken walls, each one straight ahead of her. Then they will be cast out toward Harmon. The walls are broken, and that's how they leave.

That's it. "Go to Bethel and transgress; rebel even more at Gilgal!" Those are the LORD's words in verse 4. It's a surprising thing to read, and it's right there in the text. Keep reading, because verse 5 comes right behind it.

Tearing down altars is not what He tells them to do in verse 4. The LORD did say earlier that He would bring destruction on the altars of Bethel (Amos 3:14), but that's a different thing. Here He says, "Go to Bethel and transgress…" That's the instruction, so you can see why this one tangles people up.

No resting here, friend. Verse 4 says to transgress at Bethel and rebel even more at Gilgal. Then it adds sacrifices every morning and tithes every three days. That's a full schedule, with no feet up.
The text says the opposite, friend. Right after the leavened bread, the LORD says, "…loudly proclaim your freewill offerings." That's loud, not quiet. Nobody is whispering these offerings.

False is right. The LORD tells them to offer leavened bread as a thank offering and to "…loudly proclaim your freewill offerings." Loud is the word, so nothing is kept quiet. The offerings are announced out loud.

explanations.answer: It's what they love to do
explanations.explanation: Yes, the LORD says it Himself: "For that is what you children of Israel love to do," declares the Lord GOD. He gives that as the reason, and the text gives no other. Love is the word He uses.
Priests don't appear anywhere in verses 4 and 5, friend. The LORD says, "For that is what you children of Israel love to do." The text puts it on what Israel loves. Nobody is pushing them.

Fear is a reasonable guess, but it's not what the verse says. The LORD says, "For that is what you children of Israel love to do," declares the Lord GOD. The word is love. I'd stick with the words He actually used.

explanations.answer: They did not return to Him
explanations.explanation: That's right. The LORD says, "…yet you did not return to Me," declares the LORD. He brought lack of bread to all their towns, and the response He names is that they did not return. You'll be hearing that line again, friend.

explanations.answer: They returned to Him in tears
explanations.explanation: The text says the opposite. The LORD says, "…yet you did not return to Me." No returning, tearful or otherwise. That one stays the same all the way through the passage.

explanations.answer: They cried out to Him for help
explanations.explanation: That sounds like a natural thing to do when bread runs short. But the verse doesn't say they cried out. It says, "…yet you did not return to Me," declares the LORD. I'd go with what He said over what feels natural.
Not quite, friend. The LORD says, "I sent rain on one city but withheld it from another." It wasn't the same everywhere. He also says that one field received rain while another without rain withered.

False is right. The LORD says, "I sent rain on one city but withheld it from another." Then He says, "One field received rain; another without rain withered." So it differed from city to city and field to field.
The text says otherwise, friend. People staggered from city to city for water to drink, "…but they were not satisfied…" So they went looking, and the water wasn't enough. That's a hard picture.

False is right. The people staggered from city to city for water to drink, "…but they were not satisfied…" They kept searching, and it didn't satisfy them. The LORD then says again, "…yet you did not return to Me."

True. The LORD says, "I struck you with blight and mildew in your growing gardens and vineyards; the locust devoured your fig and olive trees…" So the gardens and vineyards were hit, and the fig and olive trees were hit too. Then comes the line we keep hearing: "…yet you did not return to Me…"

It's actually True, friend. After the blight and mildew, the LORD says, "…the locust devoured your fig and olive trees…" So the trees were hit as well. And the same line follows: "…yet you did not return to Me…"
That's it. The LORD says, "I sent plagues among you like those of Egypt…" He picks Egypt as the comparison. It's a heavy verse, and it ends with the same sad line: "…yet you did not return to Me…"
Moab isn't named anywhere in this verse, friend. The LORD says, "I sent plagues among you like those of Egypt…" The comparison is Egypt. Go back to that line and it's right there.
Edom doesn't show up in verse 10, friend. The verse says, "I sent plagues among you like those of Egypt…" Egypt is the land the LORD names. Keep your eyes on that word when you read it again.
Yes. The LORD says, "I filled your nostrils with the stench of your camp…" This is a heavy part of the passage, so no jokes from me here. It still ends the same way: "…yet you did not return to Me…"

Smoke and altars were all over the earlier verses, so I see how that one pulled you. But in verse 10 the LORD says, "I filled your nostrils with the stench of your camp…" The camp is what He names. This is a heavy verse, so take it slowly.

The verse doesn't mention dust or a desert. The LORD says, "I filled your nostrils with the stench of your camp…" The camp is the place He names. It's a heavy verse, and the text says nothing more than that.

That's right. The LORD says, "Some of you I overthrew as I overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah…" He ties what happened to Israel to those two cities. Then He says they were like a firebrand snatched from a blaze, and still, "…yet you did not return to Me…"

Nineveh and Babylon are big names, but verse 11 doesn't use them. The LORD says, "Some of you I overthrew as I overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah…" Those are the two cities He names. Both are in that one line.

Tyre and Sidon don't appear in this verse, friend. The LORD says He overthrew some of them as He overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah. Those are the two cities He names. Check the verse and the answer is right there.
Yes. The LORD says, "…prepare to meet your God, O Israel!" That's the command after everything He listed. It's the line the whole passage has been leading to, so it's good to see it land.

Broken walls came up back in verse 3, so I see why this one pulled you. But in verse 12 the LORD tells Israel, "…prepare to meet your God, O Israel!" He doesn't mention rebuilding. The command is to prepare.
Bashan came up in verse 1 with the cows, but it's not in verse 12. The LORD says, "…prepare to meet your God, O Israel!" There's no hiding in that command. Israel is told to prepare.

The text says the opposite, friend. Verse 13 says He "…reveals His thoughts to man…" So His thoughts aren't hidden from people. That line comes right after He forms the mountains and creates the wind.
False is right. Verse 13 says that He "…reveals His thoughts to man…" He shows them to people instead of keeping them hidden. Same verse, same God who forms the mountains and creates the wind.
True. Verse 13 says He "…turns the dawn to darkness…" It sits right beside the mountains and the wind in that list. Then it finishes with His name: the LORD, the God of Hosts.
It's actually True, friend. Verse 13 says He "…turns the dawn to darkness…" That's in the same verse as the mountains and the wind. Then comes His name: the LORD, the God of Hosts.
